newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa wage rises on par with inflation in H1.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa wage rises on par with inflation in H1.

text.p: South African wage settlements during the first six months of the year averaged 9.7 percent, running neck and neck with the average inflation rate for the year to date, a survey released on Monday said.
But wage settlement levels were seen overtaking inflation with the expected year-end figure close to the 9.9 percent level recorded last year.

A quarterly wage settlement report up to June 30 by industrial relations consultants Andrew Levy & Associates showed rises ranged from 6.8 percent to 15 percent across industries with the average minimum wage level at 1,650 rand.
Last year's first half average was 10.4 percent.
Andrew Levy research associate Jackie Kelly said initial union wage demands ranged from a low of eight percent to 146 percent.
Management counter-offers ranged from nought percent to 11 percent with an average of 6.2 percent.
In 54.3 percent of cases, wage negotiations were settled without industrial action and in 16.1 percent of cases strike action took place.

Third party intervention, in the form of the recently formed dispute resolution service, the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration and the Independent Mediation Services of South Africa, took place in 20.8 percent of wage negotiations.
Average settlements reached with the major unions included 11.4 percent with the National Union of Mineworkers and 9.5 percent with the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa.
Kelly also said 57.9 percent of companies surveyed operated a 40-hour working week, with 24.1 percent working 45-48 hours per week.

The controversial new Basic Conditions of Employment Bill, which was tabled by cabinet in April and still needs to be passed by parliament, makes provision for a maximum 45 hour working week, reduced from 46, in many sectors.
It proposes a large reduction in working hours for security workers from 60 hours a week to 45 hours.
The 1.9-million member Congress of South African Trade Unions is pushing for a 40-hour working week, phased in over not more than five years, to be included in the new labour law.
